analysis.one_liner: Bans brand-name drug companies from paying generic drug makers to keep cheaper generic versions off the market.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee without a single amendment in February 2007 and was placed on the Senate calendar, but it never received a Senate floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drug company challenges a brand-name drug's patent, the two companies sometimes settle with a deal: the brand pays the generic company money or other value, and the generic company agrees to delay selling its cheaper version for months or years. The Federal Trade Commission found this happening in most recent settlements. This bill would make those 'pay for delay' deals illegal under antitrust law, require companies to certify under penalty of perjury that they disclose all side agreements to the government, and strip a generic company of its special 180-day marketing exclusivity if it cuts such a deal. The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it, but the full Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, employers, and government health programs that buy prescription drugs. Generic drugs cost 63 percent less on average than brand-name versions, per the bill's own findings, and they made up 56 percent of prescriptions but only 13 percent of drug spending [S4]. Ending pay-for-delay deals would let cheaper generics reach the market years sooner. Generic drug makers that compete on price, rather than taking payments to stay out, also stand to gain earlier market entry.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful under the Clayton Act for a brand-name drug maker to give a generic applicant anything of value in exchange for an agreement not to market the generic for any period, with an exception only for settlements that grant nothing more than the right to market the generic before the patent expires [S4].

Requires the CEOs or negotiating officials of brand and generic companies to certify under penalty of perjury that every agreement filed with the FTC and Justice Department is complete and includes all side deals and oral promises, closing the door on hidden payments [S4].
Strips a generic company of its valuable 180-day marketing exclusivity if a court or the FTC finally finds its settlement violated the new ban, removing the reward for cutting such deals [S4].
Directs the FTC to study how common these anticompetitive agreements were over the previous five years and report to Congress with enforcement recommendations [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose the ability to pay generic rivals to delay competition and would face tighter disclosure rules. Some generic manufacturers would also lose a source of settlement income. The bill authorizes spending for FTC enforcement [S4].

drawbacks.text: The bill outlaws not only cash payments but any 'thing of value' given to a generic filer in exchange for delayed entry, which goes beyond the narrow exclusion for settlements that grant only an early-entry license. Brand companies argued such settlements are a legitimate way to resolve patent litigation, and federal appellate courts had in fact upheld them in 2005 before this bill sought to reverse that rule by statute [S4].

A blanket ban on compensated delay settlements could push more patent disputes into full courtroom litigation instead of settlement, raising legal costs for both sides and delaying resolution case by case — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge even while accepting it to stop the pay-for-delay pattern the FTC documented [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance the bill's benefits outweigh its costs. Every dollar a brand-name company pays a generic company to stay off the market is eventually recovered from patients, employers, and government health programs through higher prices, so banning the practice targets a direct transfer from the public to two firms per drug. The main honest objections are that it narrows the traditional freedom to settle patent disputes by any means, and that some patent challenges are weak enough that keeping a brand drug on the market was not clearly wrong. Those are costs worth naming, but they are outweighed by the scale of the price impact: generics cost 63 percent less on average, and pay-for-delay deals were spreading rapidly after the 2005 court decisions [S4].

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it and it sat on the Senate's calendar of pending business for the rest of the Congress, but the Senate never voted on it and it expired in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced January 17, 2007 with an unusually bipartisan group behind it — Democrat Herb Kohl joined by Republican Charles Grassley along with Leahy, Schumer, Feingold, Kennedy, and Durbin [S6].

The Judiciary Committee held hearings and approved the bill favorably on February 15, 2007, reporting it without amendment on February 27 and placing it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 59) [S6].
No further action followed: the bill was never called up for a Senate floor vote, and the 110th Congress ended January 3, 2009 with the bill still on the calendar [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because the deals the FTC found spreading in 2006 — paying generic rivals to delay competition — remained lawful and profitable. Consumers are worse off, since generics that average 63 percent less than brand drugs kept coming to market later.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start: its seven original sponsors included six Democrats and Republican Charles Grassley of Iowa, and its 10 cosponsors split 9 Democrats to 1 Republican; the bill died on the calendar rather than in a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill directly prohibits the practice the FTC found spreading: paying generic challengers to delay competition, which let brands keep charging brand-name prices long after patent challenges were filed [S4]. Consumers eventually pay for those deals through higher drug prices, so the industry's interest here runs against the public's.

The bill takes away the option of being paid to stay off the market, but it protects the generic firms' core business: early entry at prices averaging 63 percent below brand prices [S4]. On net it pushes the industry back toward competing on price, which aligns it with consumers.
